title: The WHO Just Endorsed a $1 Antibiotic Pill That Prevents Syphilis and Chlamydia After Sex. It Is Their First Recommendation of Its Kind.
excerpt: Doxycycline post-exposure prophylaxis can reduce syphilis and chlamydia by up to 80 per cent. With STI rates rising sharply in India and across the diaspora, the decision could reshape sexual health prevention worldwide.
body:
For decades, the public health playbook for sexually transmitted infections has relied on a short list: condoms, testing, and treatment after the fact. On May 26, the World Health Organization added a new line to that playbook — one that costs less than a dollar a dose.

The WHO has issued its first-ever recommendation endorsing doxycycline post-exposure prophylaxis, commonly known as doxyPEP, as a preventive measure against bacterial sexually transmitted infections. The guidance recommends that men who have sex with men and transgender women take a single 200mg dose of doxycycline within 72 hours of sexual exposure to reduce their risk of acquiring syphilis, chlamydia, and in some settings, gonorrhoea.

The evidence behind the recommendation is substantial. Two randomised clinical trials — the DoxyPEP study in Seattle and San Francisco and the DOXYVAC study in France — demonstrated that doxyPEP reduced the risk of chlamydia and early syphilis by approximately 80 per cent overall. Gonorrhoea reduction was more modest, around 33 to 55 per cent, depending on local antibiotic resistance patterns.

## Why This Matters for the Indian Diaspora

India reported an estimated 70 million new cases of curable STIs in 2020, according to the WHO's global surveillance data. Syphilis rates among Indian men have risen 40 per cent in the last decade, and chlamydia remains dramatically underdiagnosed because most infections produce no symptoms. These numbers track closely with the broader South Asian population in the US, UK, and Canada, where STI rates among men in urban centres have been climbing steadily.

The stigma around STI testing in South Asian communities is well documented. A 2024 survey of South Asian men in the UK found that fewer than a third had been tested for STIs in the previous year, compared with nearly half of White British men. A prevention tool that works after exposure — quietly, cheaply, and without requiring a clinic visit — could reach populations that traditional screening campaigns have missed.

## How DoxyPEP Works

Doxycycline is a tetracycline antibiotic that has been used for over 60 years. It is cheap, widely available, and carries a well-understood side-effect profile. The most common effects are mild gastrointestinal discomfort and photosensitivity. It is taken as a single 200mg dose as soon as possible after unprotected sex, ideally within 24 hours and no later than 72 hours.

The mechanism is straightforward: the antibiotic reaches sufficient tissue concentration to kill syphilis and chlamydia bacteria before they establish infection. For gonorrhoea, effectiveness varies because resistance to tetracycline antibiotics is more common in Neisseria gonorrhoeae.

## The Antimicrobial Resistance Question

The WHO's recommendation comes with a significant caveat. Widespread use of doxycycline as a prophylactic raises legitimate concerns about accelerating antimicrobial resistance. The WHO emphasised that implementation should be part of a comprehensive sexual health approach, should prioritise people with recent or recurrent STIs, and must include context-appropriate monitoring of resistance patterns.

Early surveillance data from San Francisco, which became the first US jurisdiction to recommend doxyPEP in 2022, has been reassuring but limited. Tetracycline resistance in gonorrhoea has not measurably increased in that population, though researchers caution that longer follow-up is needed.

## What It Costs

In the US, a 30-day supply of generic doxycycline costs between $4 and $15 without insurance. In India, a single 200mg dose costs less than 10 rupees, roughly 12 cents. For public health systems in countries with rising STI burdens, the cost-effectiveness calculation is striking: preventing a single case of congenital syphilis — which can cause stillbirth, blindness, and neurological damage in newborns — saves thousands of dollars in neonatal care.

The CDC issued its own doxyPEP guidelines in 2024. The WHO recommendation now provides a global framework that could accelerate adoption in India, Southeast Asia, and sub-Saharan Africa, where STI burdens are highest and prevention infrastructure is thinnest.

For diaspora families navigating sexual health conversations across cultural and generational divides, the existence of a simple, evidence-backed prevention tool may lower the barrier to having those conversations at all.
